rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the supplied facts and tells the founder where the land mines are. Its strongest line, "Liquid Death says it's profitable on contribution margin — but won't show net profit," is a real skeptical business angle with the right proof burden. B has the sharper flagship frame in "Liquid Death bets a flagship store can do what 120,000 grocery aisles can't," but then it blows trust with "sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now," which is not in the update.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death opens its first permanent store as it converts to a B Corp" jams two separate stories into one headline; the retail angle gets muddier, not stronger.
"DTC-native and 'anti-marketing' brands" and "viral video" lean on brand lore not supplied in the update. Probably true in the real world, but this exercise asked for traceable grounding.
"$4.2M to clean-water nonprofits" is a weaker standalone angle than A admits. Without recipients, dates, or a denominator, it belongs under the B Corp/accountability story, not as its own full lane.
gaps_in_B: "Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now" is invented. The update says limited-edition canned water, not store-exclusive water, not a launch, and not unavailable elsewhere.

"a store-exclusive can" and "The limited-edition can launches alongside the store opening" turn a thin merch/store fact into a product-pipeline story. That is exactly the sort of confident extrapolation that gets a founder embarrassed.
"near-total retail penetration" and "already everywhere" overstate ~120,000 retail doors without a market denominator. Strong tension, sloppy wording.
The product angle duplicates the store angle while pretending to be a separate beverage-trade story. It needs proof before it deserves a headline, not after.
